qs.q: A 35-year-old man with no bleeding symptoms is undergoing a pre-operative evaluation for hernia repair. Laboratory tests show a normal PT but a prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT). Which factor deficiency is the most likely cause?
qs.e: Factor XII deficiency causes prolonged PTT but normal PT, and characteristically does not cause clinical bleeding symptoms. Factor VIII deficiency would present with significant bleeding tendencies.
qs.s: Chemical Pathology — Study Notes — Hematopathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 20-year-old man actively bleeding during surgery has a low hemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, and both prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times. Which blood product provides red cells, platelets, and clotting factors simultaneously?
qs.e: Whole blood is the appropriate comprehensive product providing red blood cells, platelets, and coagulation factors all in one. Other choices like cryoprecipitate only supply specific replacement factors.

qs.q: A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent joint bleeds. His prothrombin time is normal, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is prolonged, thrombin time (TT) is normal. Which coagulation factor abnormality is most likely?
o: Congenital deficiency of plasma Factor VII
Congenital deficiency of plasma Factor VIII
Acquired deficiency of systemic Vitamin K
qs.e: An isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT and TT, plus haemarthroses, is classic for haemophilia A.

qs.q: A 35-year-old man has no clinical evidence for bleeding and he feels fine. As part of a pre-operative workup for a hernia repair, laboratory studies show Hgb 14.8 g/dL, Hct 45%, MCV 96 fL, WBC count 8500/microliter, and platelet count 275,000/microliter. His prothrombin time is normal, but the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. A deficiency of which of the following coagulation factors is m
qs.e: An isolated prolonged PTT with a normal PT and no clinical bleeding history typically indicates a deficiency in a factor involved solely in the intrinsic pathway, such as Factor XII, prekallikrein, or high molecular weight kininogen. Factor XII deficiency is the most common of these and does not usually cause bleeding symptoms.

qs.q: A 20-year-old man is actively bleeding from multiple sites during surgery. He has a CBC that shows a WBC count of 4500/microliter, Hgb 7.6 g/dL, Hct 23.9%, MCV 98 fL, and platelet count 75,000/microliter. His prothrombin time is 30 seconds and partial thromboplastin time 63 seconds. What is the best blood product to use for him in this situation?
o: Administer packed red cells together with fresh frozen plasma.
qs.e: The patient has anemia (low Hgb), thrombocytopenia (low platelets), and prolonged PT/PTT (coagulopathy). This indicates a need for both red blood cells to improve oxygen-carrying capacity (addressed by PRBCs) and coagulation factors to correct the bleeding diathesis (addressed by FFP, which contains all coagulation factors).

qs.q: A 12-year-old boy has had multiple episodes of bleeding since infancy. It is characterized by hemarthroses and decreased joint mobility. His prothrombin time (PT) is normal, but the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) is elevated. When his plasma is mixed with normal plasma, the PTT is not elevated. His platelet count is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause for his illness?
qs.e: Hemarthroses (joint bleeding), normal PT, elevated PTT, normal platelet count, and correction of PTT upon mixing with normal plasma are classic findings of a congenital intrinsic pathway factor deficiency, most commonly Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) or Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency). Hemophilia A is the most common severe form.

qs.q: A 33-year-old woman has had multiple episodes of deep venous thrombosis over the past year. Last week she had a transient ischemic attack. On examination there are no abnormal findings. Laboratory studies show a prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time. When her plasma is mixed in a ratio of 1:1 with normal plasma, neither the PT nor the PTT normalize. Which of the following condition
qs.e: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies, which can lead to recurrent arterial and venous thrombosis, and pregnancy morbidity. The prolonged PT and PTT that do not correct upon mixing with normal plasma is a characteristic finding in some patients with APS due to the presence of lupus anticoagulants, which interfere with the clotting assays

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) measures the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways. It is used to screen for bleeding disorders and to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy.

sections.p: aPTT is a laboratory test that records the time (seconds) for plasma to clot after adding phospholipid, an activator, and calcium. Normal range is roughly 25‑35 s, but each lab sets its own reference.
b: Prolonged aPTT suggests a defect in factors VIII, IX, XI, XII, prekallikrein, high‑molecular‑weight kininogen, or common pathway factors (II, V, X).
Shortened aPTT is rare and may indicate high factor VIII levels or laboratory error.

t.b: Is the intrinsic pathway prolonged? – A result > 35 s indicates a possible factor deficiency, inhibitor, or heparin effect.

sections.p: There is no formal staging; clinicians grade severity by the degree of prolongation and associated bleeding risk.
b: Mild: 1‑1.5× upper limit of normal (ULN); usually asymptomatic.
Moderate: 1.5‑2× ULN; may cause easy bruising or mucosal bleeding.
Severe: >2× ULN; high risk of spontaneous hemorrhage.

sections.p: Identify whether the abnormality is due to a factor deficiency, an inhibitor, or medication.
b: Factor deficiencies: hemophilia A (VIII), hemophilia B (IX), rare factor XI deficiency.
Acquired inhibitors: lupus anticoagulant, specific factor VIII inhibitor.
Heparin therapy (unfractionated heparin, LMWH high dose).
Liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation, severe infection (e.g., sepsis, malaria).
Vitamin K deficiency (affects common pathway, may modestly prolong aPTT).
Herbal remedies containing coumarins or quinine.

sections.p: Patients may present with mucosal bleeding, hemarthroses, or prolonged bleeding after minor trauma. In anticoagulated patients, bleeding risk correlates with aPTT length.
b: Spontaneous joint or muscle bleeds suggest hemophilia.
Bruising, epistaxis, or menorrhagia point to acquired inhibitors.
Bleeding after surgery or catheter removal may indicate excess heparin.

sections.p: A stepwise approach clarifies the cause of a prolonged aPTT.
b: Repeat aPTT to exclude lab error.
Mixing study (patient plasma + normal plasma) distinguishes deficiency vs inhibitor.
Specific factor assays if deficiency suspected.
Lupus anticoagulant panel if inhibitor suspected.
Heparin level or anti‑Xa assay when heparin therapy is possible.

t.b: Does the aPTT correct with normal plasma? – Corrected: factor deficiency; unchanged: inhibitor present.
Is factor VIII low? – Low level confirms hemophilia A or acquired deficiency.
Is a phospholipid‑dependent inhibitor present? – Positive suggests antiphospholipid syndrome.

sections.p: Severe prolongation can lead to life‑threatening hemorrhage, especially intracranial or intra‑abdominal.
b: Uncontrolled bleeding after minor injury.
Rapid drop in hemoglobin or hemodynamic instability.
Concurrent D‑dimer elevation suggesting consumptive coagulopathy.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide hemostatic support.
b: Replace deficient factors with plasma, cryoprecipitate, or recombinant factor concentrates.
Use bypassing agents (e.g., activated prothrombin complex) for inhibitor‑mediated hemophilia.
Stop or reverse heparin with protamine if iatrogenic.
Treat underlying infection (malaria, TB, HIV) or liver disease.
Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs that worsen bleeding.

sections.p: Monitor aPTT after treatment to ensure correction and prevent recurrence.
b: Re‑check aPTT 6‑12 h after factor replacement or heparin reversal.
Educate patients with hemophilia on safe activities and prompt treatment of injuries.
Screen family members for inherited deficiencies.

sections.p: aPTT is frequently mixed up with PT/INR or thrombin time.
b: PT/INR assesses the extrinsic pathway (factor VII, tissue factor).
Thrombin time evaluates conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, not factor deficiencies.

sections.p: Certain conditions may give a normal aPTT despite a bleeding tendency.
b: Low‑level factor VIII elevation in acute phase reaction shortens aPTT.
Heparin contamination of the sample can falsely prolong aPTT.
Lupus anticoagulant may prolong aPTT but paradoxically increase thrombosis risk.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache or neurological change suggesting intracranial hemorrhage
Rapid drop in blood pressure or hemoglobin

faq.q: Why is aPTT used to monitor unfractionated heparin?
faq.a: Heparin potentiates antithrombin, which mainly inhibits intrinsic pathway factors; aPTT reflects this effect.

faq.q: Can a normal aPTT rule out hemophilia?
faq.a: No; mild hemophilia may have a normal aPTT, especially if factor levels are >30 %.

faq.q: What does a mixing study that does not correct indicate?
faq.a: The presence of an inhibitor, such as a lupus anticoagulant or specific factor inhibitor.
